title: Hybridization Involving s and p Orbitals
topicTitle: Hybridization involving s and p orbitals only
notes: **Hybridization concept:** When atoms form molecules, their valence atomic orbitals (of similar energy) mix to form new equivalent orbitals called hybrid orbitals. These hybrids have different shapes and orientations than the parent orbitals and point toward the bonded atoms, minimizing electron-pair repulsion. The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed.

**sp hybridization:** One s + one p orbital → two sp hybrid orbitals oriented 180° apart (linear geometry). The two unhybridized p orbitals remain perpendicular to the sp axis. Examples: BeCl₂ (Be: $[He]\, 2s^2 \rightarrow 2s^1\, 2p^1$ after promotion, then sp hybridization), CO₂ (central C is sp hybridized), HC≡CH (each C is sp hybridized). In CO₂, each C=O bond has one $\sigma$ (sp–p overlap) and one $\pi$ (unhybridized p–p overlap).

**sp² hybridization:** One s + two p orbitals → three sp² hybrid orbitals in a trigonal planar arrangement (120° apart). One unhybridized p orbital remains perpendicular to the plane. Examples: BF₃ (B: $[He]\, 2s^2\, 2p^1 \rightarrow$ sp², empty p orbital accepts electron pair → Lewis acid), C₂H₄ (each C is sp²; the C=C $\pi$ bond uses the unhybridized p orbitals), benzene C₆H₆ (all C are sp², forming a delocalized $\pi$ system).

**sp³ hybridization:** One s + three p orbitals → four sp³ hybrid orbitals directed toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron (109.5° bond angle). Examples: CH₄ (C: sp³, four C–H $\sigma$ bonds), NH₃ (N: sp³, three bonds + one lone pair → bond angle 107° due to lone pair repulsion), H₂O (O: sp³, two bonds + two lone pairs → bond angle 104.5°). The decrease from 109.5° follows VSEPR: lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.

**Determining hybridization from steric number:** Hybridization = steric number (SN) of the central atom. SN = number of sigma bonds + number of lone pairs on the central atom. SN = 2 → sp, SN = 3 → sp², SN = 4 → sp³. For example, in SO₂, S has 2 sigma bonds + 1 lone pair = SN = 3 → sp². In NH₄⁺, N has 4 sigma bonds + 0 lone pairs = SN = 4 → sp³.

**Why hybridize — the carbon paradox:** Ground-state carbon ($1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^2$) has only two unpaired electrons and should form only two bonds. Yet carbon consistently forms four bonds (e.g., CH₄). Hybridization resolves this: one 2s electron is promoted to 2p, giving $2s^1\, 2p^3$, and the four orbitals hybridize to four equivalent sp³ orbitals, each with one unpaired electron. The energy invested in promotion is more than recovered by forming two extra bonds.

**Hybridization and bond angles:** The ideal bond angles for each hybridization are: sp = 180°, sp² = 120°, sp³ = 109.5°. Deviations occur when lone pairs are present (NH₃: 107°, H₂O: 104.5°) or when substituents have different sizes/electronegativities (e.g., CF₄ has slightly different angles than CH₄ due to fluorine's larger size).

**s-character and electronegativity:** The percentage s-character in a hybrid orbital affects the atom's effective electronegativity. sp (50% s) > sp² (33% s) > sp³ (25% s). More s-character means the electrons are held closer to the nucleus, making the atom more electronegative. This explains why terminal alkynes (sp C–H) are more acidic than alkenes (sp² C–H) or alkanes (sp³ C–H).

**Bond length vs. s-character:** Greater s-character leads to shorter, stronger bonds because s orbitals are closer to the nucleus. C–H bond lengths: sp C–H (106 pm) < sp² C–H (108 pm) < sp³ C–H (109 pm). Similarly, C–C bond lengths: C≡C (120 pm) < C=C (134 pm) < C–C (154 pm).

**Double bonds and hybridization:** A double bond always contains one $\sigma$ bond (from hybrid orbital overlap) and one $\pi$ bond (from unhybridized p orbital overlap). The atom involved in a double bond must have at least one unhybridized p orbital, so it cannot be sp³ hybridized. For example, the carbon in C₂H₄ is sp² (has one unhybridized p for the $\pi$ bond), while the carbon in CH₄ is sp³ (no p orbitals left unhybridized).

**Resonance and equivalent hybridization:** In molecules with resonance (e.g., carbonate CO₃²⁻, ozone O₃), all equivalent atoms have the same hybridization. In CO₃²⁻, the central carbon is sp² with three equivalent C–O bonds (bond order 1.33) — the $\pi$ electrons are delocalized over all three O atoms, not localized in any one bond.

**Orbital diagrams for common molecules:** (i) BeCl₂: Be(sp) + 2×Cl(3p) → two $\sigma$ bonds, linear. (ii) BF₃: B(sp²) + 3×F(2p) → three $\sigma$ bonds, trigonal planar; empty B p orbital makes it a Lewis acid. (iii) CH₄: C(sp³) + 4×H(1s) → four equivalent $\sigma$ bonds, tetrahedral. (iv) C₂H₂: each C(sp) + H(1s) + C(sp) → linear $\sigma$ framework; two sets of p–p $\pi$ overlap give two $\pi$ bonds.

**Geometry prediction using hybridization:** Given a molecule, determine the central atom's steric number, assign hybridization, then predict geometry: sp → linear (180°), sp² → trigonal planar (120°), sp³ → tetrahedral (109.5°). For molecules with lone pairs, the molecular geometry differs from the electron-pair geometry (e.g., sp³ with 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal; sp³ with 2 lone pairs → bent/V-shaped).

**Limitations of hybridization theory:** (1) It is an approximation — real orbitals are not perfect hybrids. (2) It cannot predict hybridization without knowing the molecular geometry first (circular reasoning). (3) It fails for transition metal complexes where d-orbital participation is significant. (4) It does not explain magnetic properties. Despite these, it remains an indispensable tool for predicting molecular shapes in main-group chemistry.

**Real-world application — drug design:** The hybridization state of atoms in a drug molecule determines its 3D shape, which must complement the target protein's binding site. For example, the sp² hybridized carbons in the benzene ring of many pharmaceuticals (aspirin, ibuprofen) create planar regions that stack via $\pi$–$\pi$ interactions with aromatic amino acids in proteins.
confusion: Hybridization describes the bonded state, not a process the atom undergoes: Students often imagine orbitals 'mixing' as a physical event. In reality, hybridization is a mathematical procedure to construct a better wave function that matches the observed molecular geometry. The atom doesn't 'decide' to hybridize — the hybrid orbitals describe the electron distribution in the bonded molecule.

Lone pairs occupy hybrid orbitals too: In H₂O, oxygen is sp³ hybridized, and the two lone pairs occupy two of the four sp³ orbitals. The bond angle compression (104.5° vs. 109.5°) is due to lone pair–lone pair repulsion being greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion (VSEPR theory), not because lone pairs are in a different type of orbital.

Not all molecules with the same formula have the same hybridization: NO₂ and CO₂ both have three atoms, but N in NO₂ is sp² (bent, SN=3 with one unpaired electron) while C in CO₂ is sp (linear, SN=2). Always calculate steric number from sigma bonds + lone pairs, not from the number of atoms.

s-character affects acidity, not just bond length: The C–H bond in ethyne (sp, 50% s-character) is more acidic (pKa ≈ 25) than in ethene (sp², pKa ≈ 44) or ethane (sp³, pKa ≈ 50) because the sp hybrid orbital holds the bonding electrons closer to the carbon nucleus, stabilizing the conjugate base (acetylide ion). This is a direct consequence of s-character, not just a bond-length effect.

Hybridization requires orbitals of comparable energy: Only orbitals close in energy hybridize effectively. The 2s and 2p of carbon (energy difference ~8 eV) hybridize well, but 2s and 3p do not. This is why we don't see sp hybridization involving n=2 and n=3 orbitals in the same atom.
practice: Determine the hybridization of the central atom in each molecule and predict the molecular geometry: (a) XeF₄, (b) SF₄, (c) I₃⁻. (Answers: XeF₄ → sp³d², square planar; SF₄ → sp³d, seesaw; I₃⁻ → sp³d, linear.) Note: these involve d-orbitals, but the steric number method is the same.

Draw the complete orbital diagram for C₂H₄ (ethene), showing all $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds. Indicate which orbitals are hybridized and which are unhybridized. Calculate the bond angles around each carbon and explain any deviations from the ideal 120°.

Explain why the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) is larger than in NF₃ (102°), even though both have sp³ hybridization and one lone pair. (Hint: Consider the electronegativity of the substituent — fluorine pulls electron density away from nitrogen, reducing bond pair–bond pair repulsion and allowing the lone pair to compress the angle more.)

Arrange the following C–H bonds in order of increasing acidity: CH₄, CH₂=CH₂, HC≡CH. Explain your answer using the concept of s-character in hybrid orbitals and the stability of the resulting carbanion.

The carbonate ion CO₃²⁻ has three equivalent C–O bonds with identical bond lengths (129 pm), intermediate between a C–O single bond (143 pm) and a C=O double bond (120 pm). Explain this using hybridization and resonance concepts. What is the hybridization of carbon in CO₃²⁻, and what is the bond order of each C–O bond?
universalFacts: Linus Pauling introduced the concept of hybridization in 1931 to reconcile VBT with the observed tetrahedral geometry of methane. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954, partly for this work.

The bond angle in diamond (109.5°, sp³ carbon) is the same as in methane — both arise from the tetrahedral arrangement of four sp³ hybrid orbitals. This geometric universality is why diamond and graphite (sp²) have such dramatically different properties.

sp hybridization produces the shortest and strongest sigma bonds among s-p hybrids because the 50% s-character holds electrons closest to the nucleus. This is why the C≡C triple bond in acetylene (120 pm) is significantly shorter than the C–C single bond in ethane (154 pm).

The term 'hybridization' comes from the word 'hybrid' — just as crossing two plant varieties produces a hybrid, mixing atomic orbitals produces a new type of orbital with properties different from either parent.

In benzene, all six carbon atoms are sp² hybridized, and the six unhybridized p orbitals overlap sideways to form a continuous $\pi$ electron cloud above and below the ring. This delocalization gives benzene its exceptional stability (resonance energy ~152 kJ/mol) and its characteristic ring current in NMR spectroscopy.
